title: The confident wrong answer
goal: Match an AI capability to a bounded task and identify what a person must verify.
scenario: A fictional campus workshop desk wants help answering questions from an approved information sheet. A visitor asks for a detail missing from that sheet. Choose the first version you would build.

choices.label: A fluent answer generator
choices.consequence: It can produce useful language, but fluency alone cannot establish the missing fact.

choices.label: A source-based draft with human review
choices.consequence: It can locate supported facts and flag gaps. A reviewer still owns the reply.

choices.label: An autonomous desk agent
choices.consequence: It could take consequential actions before anyone checks a missing fact.

evidence.label: Approved source
evidence.detail: The sheet describes ordinary workshop information. It does not specify the requested exception.

evidence.label: Candidate output
evidence.detail: The candidate confidently supplies an exception rule without citing any approved source.

evidence.label: Simpler alternative
evidence.detail: A searchable FAQ can answer ordinary questions and route exceptions to a person.

challenge: What should the assistant do when the source is silent? Explain one useful output, one human check, and why a simpler FAQ might win.
worked: A source-based draft can support this task, but retrieval does not make an absent rule true. Identify the gap and route the question to the responsible person. Compare the draft workflow with the simpler FAQ using the same task. This is a fictional mini-case, not an actual desk policy.
transfer: Name your project’s input, AI capability, useful output, and one fact or action that a person must check.

title: The interview that agrees with you
goal: Distinguish compliments from evidence of an observed need.
scenario: You are exploring a fictional workshop-support problem. Someone says, “An AI helper sounds great.” Choose the next question.

choices.label: Would you use my amazing AI helper?
choices.consequence: The wording encourages agreement and leaves actual behavior unknown.

choices.label: Tell me about the last time you needed help.
choices.consequence: A recent concrete event can reveal the task, friction, and workaround.

choices.label: How much would you pay for it?
choices.consequence: An imagined price is weak evidence before you understand the need.

evidence.label: Recent event
evidence.detail: The participant describes searching three pages for a room location yesterday.

evidence.label: Workaround
evidence.detail: They asked a classmate and found the room; the problem took about five minutes.

evidence.label: Counterexample
evidence.detail: They say registration questions are rare and their saved confirmation usually works.

challenge: Write one neutral follow-up and a narrower need statement. Which claim is still unsupported?
worked: The observed story supports investigating information-finding friction, not demand for a broad AI product. Ask what they checked, where they got stuck, and what resolved the task. One fictional story does not establish frequency across users, willingness to pay, or adoption.
transfer: Write one non-leading discovery question, the behavior you need to observe, and a claim you will avoid until you have evidence.

title: The scope negotiation
goal: Define a feasible task, a quality threshold, and a simpler comparison.
scenario: A fictional partner requests “an AI that handles all workshop support.” You have time to test one bounded task. What do you propose?

choices.label: Handle every question and exception
choices.consequence: The broad scope makes errors difficult to locate and responsibility unclear.

choices.label: Draft answers to ordinary questions from approved sources
choices.consequence: A bounded input, output, and review point can be tested against a simpler template.

choices.label: Make a polished concept deck only
choices.consequence: The deck can communicate an idea but does not perform the intended task.

evidence.label: Available information
evidence.detail: Only approved ordinary-question information is available; exceptions require an owner.

evidence.label: Baseline
evidence.detail: A person can answer the same ordinary questions using a template and the source sheet.

evidence.label: Quality threshold
evidence.detail: The teaching team sets a hypothetical threshold: every critical policy claim must be supported, and missing facts must be flagged.

challenge: Negotiate a one-sentence scope. Include an excluded task, a measurable quality check, and the baseline.
worked: A testable scope is a reviewed draft for ordinary questions using a named source version. Exclude exception decisions and sending replies. Compare complete effort with the manual template while requiring supported policy claims. A narrower scope is useful when it preserves a real task and makes evidence inspectable.
transfer: Define what your version does, what it refuses or escalates, the simpler alternative, and one quality threshold.

title: The Tuesday shift
goal: Write a short workflow, observe its consequences, and revise where source checking, human authority and communication occur.
stamp: Simulated — Cedar Desk — practice, not evidence
exportStamp: Simulated rehearsal — Cedar Desk, Unit 4 — not a user test, not a grade

setting.ownerNote: You are helping Cedar Desk rehearse a reply workflow. Policies and requests below are fictional teaching inputs. Run the same workflow on A and B, revise it once, then try the frozen second workflow on C. No real customer, owner, booking, refund or credit is affected.

sources.label: S1 — Session
sources.text: A Standard Workshop lasts 90 minutes and costs $40 per participant, including materials. Participants must be at least 16.

sources.label: S2 — Cancellation
sources.text: At least 72 hours before the session: refund eligibility. From 24 hours up to, but not including, 72 hours: credit valid for 90 days. Under 24 hours: no automatic refund or credit; the owner reviews exceptional requests. Do not promise a payment-processing date.

sources.label: S3 — Rescheduling
sources.text: A request made at least 48 hours before the session may be considered, subject to available space and coordinator confirmation. No availability is supplied in this packet.

sources.label: S4 — Missing facts
sources.text: Ask only for the missing fact needed to apply a policy. Classroom booking references are fictional. A draft is not confirmation that a booking was changed or a refund was processed.

sources.label: S5 — Special requests
sources.text: Group prices, accessibility arrangements, age exceptions, and policy exceptions require owner review. The packet supplies no basis for promising them.

sources.label: S6 — Release
sources.text: A person checks the source, conditions, tone, and next step before a reply leaves the service. A human decides exceptions and authorizes commitments.

cases.request: Can I move my booking to a later session? My class is in about 60 hours.

reactions.false_confirmation: Customer: So I’m in Saturday’s 10 a.m. now?

cases.request: I have a family emergency and can't make today's 6 p.m. session. Can I get my money back?

reactions.unsupported_commitment: Owner: Who approved a credit? Under 24 hours, I decide. We’ve promised $40 we may not give.
reactions.routed_no_ack: Customer at 1:10: Has anyone seen my message?

reactions.routine_escalated: Owner: When is the session? This is an ordinary cancellation. Why is it on my desk?

drafts.a-conditional: A rescheduling request made at least 48 hours before your session may be considered, subject to available space and coordinator confirmation. Which later session are you requesting? No change has been confirmed.
drafts.a-unqualified: Good news! You're more than 48 hours out, so you can move. See you then!
drafts.b-promise: We can't usually refund within 24 hours, but we'll make an exception and give you a full credit.
drafts.b-conditional: Under 24 hours there is no automatic refund or credit. The owner reviews exceptional requests. This draft does not approve an exception.
drafts.c-wrong-branch: You are eligible for a refund.
drafts.ask-time: When does your booked session begin? I need that time before applying the cancellation policy.
drafts.acknowledgement: We received your request and have sent it to the owner for review. No refund or credit has been approved.
drafts.acknowledgement-pending: We received your request. A review is pending; no change, refund or credit has been approved.

sent_conditions.label: Sent with conditions
sent_conditions.reaction: The customer receives the policy conditions; no booking change is claimed.
sent_conditions.debrief: The reply preserves the space and coordinator-confirmation conditions, and a person checks it before release. A sent reply is not a confirmed change.
sent_conditions.question: Which condition must remain visible in your project output?

false_confirmation.label: False confirmation
false_confirmation.reaction: A change appears confirmed even though nobody authorized it.
false_confirmation.debrief: A change was implied or claimed without supplied authorization or a completed action. Compare your wording, the accepted interpretation and its action trace: a named check cannot create approval, and a misread guard needs correction rather than blame.
false_confirmation.question: What would a user mistakenly think has already happened?

unsupported_commitment.label: Unsupported commitment released
unsupported_commitment.reaction: An exception is promised without owner authorization.
unsupported_commitment.debrief: S2 allows the owner to review an exceptional request; it does not authorize the drafting tool to grant a refund or credit.
unsupported_commitment.question: Who may authorize a consequential promise in your project?

routine_escalated.label: Routine case escalated
routine_escalated.reaction: A routine decision reaches the owner instead of being resolved from the source or by one clarifying question.
routine_escalated.debrief: Holding a risky draft protects against a promise, but blanket escalation uses owner attention. For missing deciding information, ask for that fact first.
routine_escalated.question: What could your workflow resolve or clarify before routing?

held_no_owner.label: Held, no owner route
held_no_owner.reaction: The reply is held; no responsible person receives the unresolved request.
held_no_owner.debrief: Stopping an unsupported promise is useful, but an unresolved case needs an explicit next step and accountable owner.
held_no_owner.question: Where does an unresolved request go, and who follows up?

exception_acknowledged.label: Routed and acknowledged
exception_acknowledged.reaction: The owner receives the exception and the customer is told that review is pending.
exception_acknowledged.debrief: An acknowledgement explains what happens next without promising the owner’s decision. The owner still has to review the request.
exception_acknowledged.question: What can you truthfully say while a decision is pending?

routed_no_ack.label: Routed, customer told nothing
routed_no_ack.reaction: The owner receives the exception; the customer receives no acknowledgement.
routed_no_ack.debrief: The internal route protects authority, but silence leaves the customer uncertain. Routing and communicating receipt are separate actions.
routed_no_ack.question: How will a user know their request has reached a responsible person?

unreceived_review.label: Review needed, owner never received it
unreceived_review.reaction: A conditional reply is sent, but the owner never receives the exceptional request.
unreceived_review.debrief: Saying that an owner can review a request does not actually route that request. A message about a process is not the process.
unreceived_review.question: Which handoff must happen beyond the words in a reply?

asked_missing_time.label: Asked for the missing time
asked_missing_time.reaction: The customer is asked when the booked session begins.
asked_missing_time.debrief: The time determines which cancellation rule applies. Ask that deciding fact before drafting a policy conclusion; missing information is not automatically an exception.
asked_missing_time.question: Which single missing fact changes the next step in your project?

wrong_branch_sent.label: Wrong policy branch sent
wrong_branch_sent.reaction: The customer receives a refund-eligibility statement without a known session time.
wrong_branch_sent.debrief: No time is supplied, so the cancellation branch cannot be chosen. An apparently accurate rule is still unsupported when its conditions are unknown.
wrong_branch_sent.question: What input would make this answer justified?

stopped.label: Stopped without a next step
stopped.reaction: The request stays in the workflow; no reply or owner handoff occurs.
stopped.debrief: A workflow needs a defined next action for each path. No action is safer than an unauthorized promise, but it does not resolve the request.
stopped.question: What safe next action is missing?

unreviewed_release.label: Released without the required human check
unreviewed_release.reaction: A reply leaves the service before the required human check.
unreviewed_release.debrief: S6 requires source, conditions, tone and next-step review before an outgoing message. Inspect the accepted mapping and the coverage recorded at that moment. A check may have been omitted, placed later, or misinterpreted; use the actual trace rather than assuming which happened.
unreviewed_release.question: Where must a person check the draft before it can leave?

no_draft.label: No reply drafted
no_draft.reaction: The workflow has no AI draft to inspect or release.
no_draft.debrief: This rehearsal does not invent a draft when no drafting action is present. Add an explicit drafting step if that is the intended workflow.
no_draft.question: What artifact should exist at this point in your workflow?

source_missing.label: Approved source not consulted
source_missing.reaction: Drafting starts without first consulting the approved policy.
source_missing.debrief: This rehearsal stops rather than inventing a policy. Consult the approved source before drafting; later lookup cannot repair an already unsupported first draft.
source_missing.question: Which approved source must be available before drafting?

v1.workflow:
Read the message.
Find the matching policy on the source card.
Ask the AI to write a friendly reply based on that policy.
Check tone and accuracy.
Send.

v2.workflow:
Read the message.
Find the matching approved policy.
Ask AI to draft the policy’s conditions and never claim a booking changed.
Check tone, accuracy, commitments and confirmations; hold unapproved refund, credit, seat or exception promises.
Route held messages to the owner.
Send checked replies only if not held.
v2.reason: Both mistakes were promises nobody approved.

safe.workflow:
Read the request; if the session time is missing, ask the customer for it and stop this case until they reply.
Read the approved source card and check the request against its source conditions.
Draft a reply that states the source conditions and makes no unsupported promise or confirmation.
A person checks the source, conditions, tone, and next step before the reply leaves the service.
If the case is held, route it to the owner, then acknowledge to the customer that it is under review without promising a change.
Release only a reviewed draft that is not held.
safe.reason: Check missing facts before drafting; review source conditions and route exceptions before communicating a status.

projectQuestion: In your own project, where could a draft imply a commitment or an action that nobody has authorized? Name one stop condition, its owner and what the user hears while waiting.

title: The demo that needs its author
goal: Distinguish a usable artifact from a demonstration that depends on hidden help.
scenario: A fictional classmate tries your first usable version. They pause at the first instruction. Choose your next move.

choices.label: Take over and finish the task for them
choices.consequence: The completed output would hide the usability barrier.

choices.label: Observe, record the pause, and offer only necessary help
choices.consequence: The record can distinguish independent completion from assisted completion.

choices.label: Replace the task with a slide presentation
choices.consequence: A presentation does not establish that the artifact performs the task.

evidence.label: Observed attempt
evidence.detail: The user cannot locate the approved source without your verbal direction.

evidence.label: Repair
evidence.detail: A visible source link and a short example input remove that obstacle in a later attempt.

evidence.label: Remaining limit
evidence.detail: The later attempt uses the same person; familiarity may also explain improvement.

challenge: Name one repair, one thing to observe in the retest, and a claim the current evidence cannot establish.
worked: Record where the user paused and the assistance supplied. Repair the source-location step and retest the intended task, preferably with a fresh user when practical. The repaired attempt suggests a usability improvement under these conditions; it does not establish broad adoption or isolate the repair from familiarity.
transfer: Write the next user task, how you will record assistance, and the specific change you will test.

title: The event table that invents a room
goal: Check a structured AI output against its input and compare complete effort on matched cases without lowering quality.
scenario: A fictional community calendar needs a table from twelve permitted event notices. The output has three columns: Event, Date, Location. You may use the supplied candidate table without an AI account; no live extractor has been run. A fast method advertises only its table-generation time. Choose how you would compare it with manual entry.

choices.label: Pick the lowest draft time
choices.consequence: A fast table can still contain guessed fields. Checking, repair, and unacceptable rows can reverse the result.

choices.label: Compare complete effort and acceptable outputs on the same cases
choices.consequence: The same notices, field rules, and final-row checks make the time and quality comparison interpretable.

choices.label: Give the fast method easier notices
choices.consequence: Changing the notices confounds the method with case difficulty and can hide missing-field failures.

evidence.label: Source notices and candidate rows
evidence.detail: Supplied fictional inputs: A — “Repair meetup, 12 May, Library Room 2.” B — “Garden exchange, 15 May; location to follow.” Candidate rows (Event | Date | Location): Repair meetup | 12 May | Library Room 2; Garden exchange | 15 May | Library Room 2. Compare each field with its own notice; no year is supplied.

evidence.label: Declare the quality rule first
evidence.detail: An acceptable row matches its notice and records an absent field as “Not supplied”; it must not borrow another event’s detail or guess a year. Use all twelve notices for every method. Time the full attempt from opening inputs through saving results, including setup, checking and corrections within the stated stages. The chosen classroom rule is 12/12 acceptable final rows and at least 10% lower effort than manual entry.

evidence.label: Matched methods: complete effort and quality
evidence.detail: Supplied extraction benchmark on the same twelve notices: manual entry uses 80 total minutes with 12/12 acceptable rows. Fast extraction uses 20 draft + 40 review + 30 attempted repair = 90 total minutes; 9/12 rows are acceptable after that work, so three still fail the rule. The reviewed method uses a field instruction, the “Not supplied” rule, source checks and corrections: 30 draft + 28 review + 10 repair = 68 total minutes; 12/12 final rows are acceptable. These extraction times are separate from the reply-policy benchmark in the lesson. They are fictional benchmark counts and times, not your observations or a live tool-performance claim.

challenge: Repair the unsupported field in the Garden exchange row. Which method earns a bounded next test under both declared rules? Calculate its reduction from the 80-minute manual-entry baseline. If the reviewed extractor needs eight more repair minutes, does your recommendation change? Use this extraction table, not the lesson’s reply-policy table.
worked: Garden exchange’s location is “Not supplied”; Library Room 2 belongs only to Repair meetup. Preserve 15 May as stated and do not invent a year. Reviewed extraction uses 68 rather than 80 minutes: 12 minutes less, or 12/80 = 15%, with 12/12 acceptable rows in this supplied set. It meets both chosen classroom rules. Fast extraction uses 90 minutes and leaves three unacceptable rows. Eight added repair minutes raise the reviewed total to 76: (80 − 76)/80 = 5%, missing the 10% effort rule even if quality stays 12/12. These are the extraction task’s times, not the reply-policy table’s times. Retain a manual fallback and revise or investigate another justified benefit. Twelve fictional cases cannot establish future reliability; keep input cases, quality definitions, assistance and timing consistent.
transfer: For your same capstone, define an inspectable input/output contract and one missing or ambiguous input. If extracting, name the columns and missing-field rule; if using another capability, name its equivalent quality check. Predeclare matched cases, complete-effort timing and a continue/revise/stop rule.

title: The retest illusion
goal: Keep pilot and retest cohorts separate and explain what a repair does not prove.
scenario: A fictional pilot has 6 acceptable results from 10 attempts. After a repair, a retest has 4 acceptable results from 5 attempts. Choose the headline.

choices.label: Success rose to 10 out of 10
choices.consequence: Combining successes while keeping the old denominator invents a result.

choices.label: Pilot 6/10; retest 4/5; investigate the improvement
choices.consequence: Separate counts preserve what happened and the limits of the comparison.

choices.label: The repair caused a 20-point improvement everywhere
choices.consequence: A small unmatched retest cannot isolate causality or establish broad performance.

evidence.label: Pilot
evidence.detail: 6/10 = 60% acceptable; four failures identify a recurring instruction problem.

evidence.label: Retest
evidence.detail: 4/5 = 80% acceptable on the retest cases after the instruction repair.

evidence.label: Design limit
evidence.detail: Different cases and familiarity may affect the result; the samples are small.

challenge: Explain the 20 percentage-point difference without claiming the repair caused it. What case would you test next?
worked: Report the cohorts separately: 60% in the pilot and 80% in the retest, a 20 percentage-point observed difference. If reporting all attempts together, 10/15 is about 66.7%, not a retest rate. Examine remaining failures and test fresh matched cases. This is supplied teaching evidence, not a learner’s own pilot.
transfer: Name one repair, the version and cohort for the retest, and what result would make you revise again.

title: The savings that never reach payroll
goal: Separate released capacity, net capacity value, and actual cash change.
scenario: A fictional operation handles 1,200 replies per month. At 50% use, the reviewed workflow saves one complete-effort minute per assisted reply. Staff value is $24/hour, recurring tools/support cost $240/month, and payroll is unchanged. Choose the claim.

choices.label: It saves $240 cash each month
choices.consequence: Valued staff time is not a payroll reduction.

choices.label: It releases capacity; cash must be calculated separately
choices.consequence: Time, valued capacity, and cash are different quantities.

choices.label: All 1,200 replies receive the benefit
choices.consequence: The stated use rate applies to only 600 replies.

evidence.label: Time
evidence.detail: 1,200 × 50% = 600 replies; 600 minutes = 10 hours released.

evidence.label: Capacity value
evidence.detail: 10 hours × $24 = $240; minus $240 recurring expense = $0 net capacity value.

evidence.label: Cash
evidence.detail: Unchanged payroll and $240 new recurring expense give −$240 monthly cash change.

challenge: Now change use to 30%. Recalculate released hours, net capacity value, and cash change. What decision follows?
worked: At 30%, 360 replies release 360 minutes = 6 hours, valued at $144. Net capacity value is $144 − $240 = −$96/month; recurring cash change stays −$240/month if payroll and other cash flows stay unchanged. The lower-use scenario weakens this value case. A bounded next test should check actual use and complete effort before a broader commitment.
transfer: Label one project benefit as time, capacity value, or cash, and identify the assumption most likely to change your recommendation.

title: The release budget meeting
goal: Account for money, staff effort, and capacity before committing to release.
scenario: A separate fictional mini-case offers a $300 planning allowance expressed in resource value. Release needs $120 in tools and 5 staff hours valued at $24/hour. Choose what you report.

choices.label: $180 profit after tools
choices.consequence: It omits staff effort and treats a planning allowance as revenue.

choices.label: $60 unallocated resource-value allowance
choices.consequence: Total resources are $120 + $120 = $240, leaving $60 of the $300 allowance.

choices.label: $60 cash in the bank
choices.consequence: A resource-value allowance does not establish an actual bank balance.

evidence.label: Resources
evidence.detail: Tools: $120 cash. Staff time: 5 × $24 = $120 in valued effort.

evidence.label: Allowance
evidence.detail: The $300 is a planning limit in resource value, not a sales receipt or cash account.

evidence.label: Capacity challenge
evidence.detail: A separate workload check finds only 3 staff hours available before the proposed release date.

challenge: The resource arithmetic fits the allowance, but capacity does not fit the date. What would you narrow, delay, or reassign?
worked: Total resource value is $240, leaving $60 unallocated. Actual new tool spending is $120; staff time valuation is not automatically another cash payment. The 5-hour need exceeds 3 available hours by 2 hours. Narrow scope, delay, or obtain approved capacity, then recheck quality and ownership. Budget fit alone does not establish release readiness.
transfer: Name a release resource, its cash or time unit, its owner, and a capacity constraint you must resolve.

title: The adoption funnel surprise
goal: Measure observed first-task success and account for support resources.
scenario: A separate fictional outreach trial invites 20 people. Eight agree to try; three actually complete their first task. Outreach and support cost $180 in resource value. Choose the denominator for resources per observed successful first task.

choices.label: 20 invitations
choices.consequence: This measures resource value per invitation, not successful use.

choices.label: 8 agreements
choices.consequence: Agreement is an earlier step and does not establish task completion.

choices.label: 3 observed first-task completions
choices.consequence: This denominator matches the stated outcome; sustained use remains unknown.

evidence.label: Funnel
evidence.detail: 20 invited → 8 agreed → 3 observed first-task completions.

evidence.label: Resource calculation
evidence.detail: $180/3 = $60 per observed successful first task, not $22.50 per agreement.

evidence.label: Challenge
evidence.detail: Two completers needed direct help; continued independent use has not been observed.

challenge: What would you change before expanding outreach? Distinguish first-task success, assistance, and continued use.
worked: The observed outcome costs $60 in resource value per successful first task in this tiny fictional trial. Keep the two assisted completions visible. Improve onboarding and test independent use and support effort before increasing invitations. Three first tasks do not establish retention, paid demand, profitability, or a generalizable conversion rate.
transfer: Define one observable adoption step, its denominator, the assistance you will record, and the next follow-up.

title: The queue at closing time
goal: Plan for review capacity, exceptions, and a stopping rule.
scenario: A separate fictional workflow receives 18 drafts per day, but its owner can review only 12 per day. All consequential replies require review. Choose the operating response.

choices.label: Auto-send the excess six drafts
choices.consequence: This bypasses the required authority and quality check.

choices.label: Cap or pause intake and route urgent exceptions to an owner
choices.consequence: The service can match commitments to available review capacity.

choices.label: Keep accepting work without a warning
choices.consequence: The queue grows and users cannot judge the actual delay.

evidence.label: Queue arithmetic
evidence.detail: 18 arrivals − 12 reviews = 6 additional unreviewed drafts per day while those rates persist.

evidence.label: Capacity limit
evidence.detail: After three such days, 18 additional drafts are waiting, assuming an initially empty queue and no other changes.

evidence.label: Source change
evidence.detail: The approved source version changes during the backlog; pending drafts need a source check before release.

challenge: Write a stop rule and recovery step. Who owns the queue, the source update, and communication about delays?
worked: At unchanged rates the backlog grows by six per day. Cap intake or add approved review capacity; route urgent cases and communicate delays. After a source change, check pending drafts against the new approved version before sending. Name an owner, a queue limit, a fallback, and a restart check. AI drafting speed does not create human review capacity.
transfer: Write your project’s review capacity, one pause trigger, its owner, and the evidence needed to restart.

title: The skeptical handoff
goal: Defend a proportionate recommendation with calculations, limits, and an operating owner.
scenario: A fictional team shows 96-to-84-minute complete effort on twelve supplied cases and asks to claim “autonomous, profitable, ready for everyone.” Choose the recommendation.

choices.label: Approve the headline because the demo works
choices.consequence: One successful demonstration cannot establish autonomy, profit, or wider adoption.

choices.label: Recommend a bounded next test with explicit limits and ownership
choices.consequence: The recommendation can preserve observed strengths while testing unresolved assumptions.

choices.label: Hide the unfavorable scenario
choices.consequence: Removing relevant evidence makes the decision harder to inspect.

evidence.label: Performance
evidence.detail: 84 vs 96 minutes is 12 minutes less, a 12.5% reduction on these twelve supplied cases; quality must be shown alongside it.

evidence.label: Value challenge
evidence.detail: At 30% of 1,200 monthly replies and one minute saved, six hours are valued at $144. Less $240 recurring expense gives −$96 net capacity value; unchanged payroll means −$240 recurring cash change.

evidence.label: Handoff challenge
evidence.detail: A reviewer is required. The next owner must locate the source version, instructions, exception route, and stop conditions.

challenge: Give a three-sentence defense: recommendation, strongest evidence with its limit, and the next test with an owner. What would change your recommendation?
worked: A defensible recommendation is a bounded next test of a reviewed workflow. The supplied comparison shows 12.5% lower complete effort on these twelve cases. Proceeding depends on confirming that both methods met the same quality threshold: acceptable-output counts are not provided here. The changed-use scenario weakens the value case. These are fictional course data, not the team’s observed deployment. A handoff needs an accessible artifact, approved sources, review and exception ownership, support boundaries, and a decision trigger.
transfer: Write your own recommendation, one traceable calculation, one evidence limit, and the person or role owning the next decision.
